stories.headline: Wall Street claws back most of a steep AI-led drop before Thanksgiving
stories.summary: U.S. stocks fell sharply early Wednesday as shares of Nvidia and other artificial-intelligence companies sold off, then recovered most of the loss by the close, though the major indexes still finished lower. Asian and European markets rose Thursday, and futures pointed to gains when U.S. trading resumes Friday.
stories.why_it_matters: A handful of AI companies now carry so much weight in the big indexes that their swings show up directly in retirement and index-fund balances. Outlets described this as the most volatile stretch for U.S. stocks in years.
stories.background: Technology and AI-related shares have been falling for several sessions as investors question how quickly heavy AI spending will turn into profits. Wednesday also brought a higher inflation reading, which reinforced expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in December, and a new round of U.S. tariff announcements. Nvidia, the chipmaker at the center of the AI trade, has been especially unsettled after its chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned in mid-November and was then reinstated. U.S. markets paused for Thanksgiving on Thursday.

facts.text: Wall Street recovered most of its early losses on Wednesday as a pullback in AI stocks eased, the Associated Press reported.
U.S. stocks still closed lower after a volatile session, according to the Wall Street Journal and the Financial Times.
During the session the Nasdaq was down about 4% and Nvidia about 8.3%, the New York Post reported; the Wall Street Journal's live coverage also noted slumps in Nvidia and Micron.
The New York Times attributed the drop to investor worries about AI, tariffs and inflation.
Oracle, CoreWeave and other technology stocks bounced back from early losses as the selloff eased before the close, MarketWatch reported.
Shares of AI company Anthropic finished higher, the Financial Times and Wall Street Journal reported.
Asian stocks rose Thursday and European indexes opened sharply higher after the late U.S. recovery.

U.S. stock futures pointed higher for Friday; the Wall Street Journal said sentiment was helped by an upward revision to third-quarter GDP and a clarification that new U.S. tariffs will replace earlier ones rather than add to them.
Deutsche Bank said the tech rout should bottom soon and forecast the S&P 500 reaching 9,000 by the end of 2027, according to MarketWatch.
Reuters reported that investors see a rising risk of a SoftBank default as pressure grows on its AI bets.

stories.headline: Fed's preferred inflation gauge rises to 3.8%, keeping a December rate increase in view
stories.summary: The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.8% in October from a year earlier, up from September, according to reports on Wednesday's release. Outlets across the spectrum said the Federal Reserve is widely expected to raise interest rates at its December meeting. Separate reports showed third-quarter economic growth revised higher and new home sales at a 10-month high.
stories.why_it_matters: Inflation near 4% means prices are still rising about twice as fast as the Fed's 2% goal, and another rate increase would push up borrowing costs on credit cards, car loans and mortgages.
stories.background: The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index is the inflation measure the Federal Reserve watches most closely when it sets interest rates. The Fed raises rates to cool spending and slow price increases, at the cost of making loans more expensive. Inflation has been climbing in recent months, and forecasters and markets had already been anticipating a December increase. Fed officials do not agree on what is driving the rise in prices, Reuters reported. The next jobs report and the Fed's December meeting are the next scheduled markers.

facts.text: The PCE price index rose 3.8% in October from a year earlier, CNBC and the New York Post reported.
The New York Post reported that the October figure was up from 3.7% in September.
The 3.8% reading matched the Dow Jones consensus forecast cited by CNBC.
The Federal Reserve is widely expected to raise interest rates next month, according to the New York Times, Fox Business and the New York Post.
Fed policymakers are at odds over the causes of high inflation, Reuters reported.
U.S. third-quarter GDP growth was revised sharply higher, Reuters and Fox Business reported.
New home sales rose 14.2% in October to a 10-month high as builders offered incentives and cut prices.
Oxford Economics said before the release that it expected a quarter-point rate increase at the December meeting.
The Fed's final 2026 policy meeting is listed for Dec. 8-9, according to Kiplinger's rundown of the Fed's schedule.
The November jobs report is scheduled for release on Friday, Dec. 4, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics calendar.
MUFG Bank said the strong U.S. economy was keeping the dollar firm despite the stock selloff, the Wall Street Journal reported.

stories.headline: White House unveils new tariff plan for trading partners; markets look past it
stories.summary: The White House on Wednesday announced a new set of tariffs aimed at more than a dozen major trading partners, while offering lower rates to countries that sign trade deals with Washington, CNBC reported. Stock markets in Asia and Europe rose afterward, and the Wall Street Journal reported a clarification that the new tariffs replace earlier ones rather than stack on top of them.
stories.why_it_matters: Tariffs are taxes on imports that can raise prices for U.S. shoppers and businesses, at a moment when inflation is already rising. Whether the new rates replace or add to existing ones determines how much costs change.
stories.background: Tariffs have been a central tool of President Trump's trade policy. The Supreme Court struck down an earlier set of his tariffs in February 2026, and in July the administration imposed replacement tariffs on about 60 trading partners. The administration has used the threat of higher rates to push other governments to sign trade agreements. Wednesday's announcement is the latest round, and several Asian governments are still in talks with Washington.

facts.text: The White House unveiled a fresh set of tariffs on Wednesday targeting more than a dozen major trading partners, CNBC reported.
CNBC reported the plan covers 14 trading partners and offers some countries lower rates if they secure trade deals with Washington.
New U.S. tariffs on China and dozens of other nations will replace rather than add to previous ones, according to a clarification reported by the Wall Street Journal.
Stocks in Asia rose Thursday as investors set aside the tariff announcement, Reuters, the Wall Street Journal and CNBC reported.
The New York Times listed tariffs alongside AI and inflation as reasons U.S. stocks fell on Wednesday.
In July 2026 the administration imposed replacement tariffs on about 60 trading partners after the Supreme Court struck down earlier tariffs in February.

stories.headline: S&P warns it may cut Nvidia's credit rating as scrutiny of Huang's return grows
stories.summary: S&P Global Ratings placed Nvidia's credit rating on watch for a possible one-notch downgrade, citing rising management and governance risk, days after Jensen Huang was reinstated as chief executive. Nvidia shares fell again Wednesday, and news outlets reported on congressional scrutiny of the reinstatement and on President Trump's personal holdings of Nvidia stock.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is one of the most heavily weighted companies in U.S. stock indexes, so turmoil in its leadership moves many people's retirement and index-fund savings. Questions about the government's role in the reinstatement are also now before Congress.
stories.background: Nvidia makes the chips that power most artificial-intelligence systems and is among the world's most valuable companies. Jensen Huang, its co-founder and longtime chief executive, resigned in mid-November; Moody's lowered its outlook on the company afterward, citing uncertainty about strategy. Huang was then reinstated as president and CEO and returned to headquarters on Monday, Nov. 23. The Trump administration supported his return, and that support, along with allegations involving China, is under scrutiny in Congress and the press.

facts.text: S&P Global placed Nvidia's rating on 'CreditWatch Negative', citing rising management and governance risks, Reuters and CNBC reported.
S&P said the rating could be cut by one notch, according to CNBC.
Nvidia shares were down 8.3% during Wednesday's session as the lift from Huang's reinstatement faded, the New York Post reported.
Huang returned to Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters on Monday, Nov. 23, apologized to employees and pledged to be a better CEO, The Hindu reported.
President Trump holds tens of millions of dollars in Nvidia shares, according to financial disclosure documents cited by CBS News.
The reinstatement has drawn scrutiny from Congress, CBS News reported; CNN reported that steps the Trump administration took to support Huang's return are also being examined.
U.S. officials are divided over Chinese spying allegations connected to the case, Reuters reported in an exclusive.
Moody's lowered its outlook on Nvidia to stable from positive after Huang's resignation while keeping its Aa1 rating, according to a Nov. 19 report.

stories.headline: FCC clears SpaceX to launch up to 1 million satellites for data centers in orbit
stories.summary: The Federal Communications Commission approved SpaceX's plan to deploy up to 1 million satellites that would serve as data centers in space for artificial-intelligence computing. The same day, Elon Musk pledged SpaceX shares for American children, a gift valued at about $18 billion.
stories.why_it_matters: The approval would allow far more satellites than have ever been in orbit, which scientists quoted by the Associated Press view skeptically, and the share pledge could put SpaceX stock into millions of children's savings accounts.
stories.background: SpaceX, led by Elon Musk, is the world's largest satellite operator through its Starlink internet service. Technology companies are spending heavily on data centers to run AI systems, and those facilities need large amounts of electricity; SpaceX proposes moving some of that computing into orbit. The FCC licenses satellite systems in the United States. Amazon, which is building a competing satellite network, opposed the plan. Trump Accounts are investment accounts for children to which companies and donors, including Michael Dell, have pledged contributions.

facts.text: The FCC authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million satellites intended to work as data centers in space.
The authorization runs through 2040, France 24 reported.
Amazon and other groups had opposed the proposal, according to CNBC.
Scientists are skeptical of the plan, the Associated Press reported.
Musk said on X that the satellites would be a "great asset to America and the world," CBS News reported.
The BBC reported that the constellation is called Starmind and is pitched as a cost- and energy-efficient way to meet demand for AI computing.
Musk pledged two SpaceX shares per child, one from the company and one from him personally, doubling an offer he made last month.
With about 72 million U.S. children under 18, the pledge is worth roughly $18 billion, according to Reuters and Daily Maverick.
SpaceX did not immediately respond to questions about whether the shares would be tied to Trump Accounts or carry a lockup period, The Hindu reported.
